These are the offspring of the dominant female and her partner, but they rely on other members to rear their young and teach them to hunt, groom each other, and defend the clan. Learn more about meerkats and their ruthless social structure: https://on.natgeo.com/hDJamX | National Geographic

item.title: More than kinship, social isolation has a greater effect on toad tadpole behavior
item.description: Amphibian larvae—often known as tadpoles—exhibit a behavior known as "social aggregation," in which they gather together to avoid predators. These interactions are evidence of their "association preferences," or their tendency to recognize members of their own species. Some varieties of tadpoles have even shown a preference for their siblings. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Tasmanian devils lived with people in outback Western Australia 45,000 years ago, new fossils show
item.description: Tasmanian devils are among Australia's most distinctive mammals. Stocky, powerful and famously noisy, wild populations are now restricted to Tasmania. But this was not always the case. In fact, thousands of years ago, devils could be found across mainland Australia. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: More US lawmakers seek new AI rules after researchers warn of human extinction
item.description: Growing numbers of U.S. lawmakers are calling for new rules to govern AI systems after dire warnings from two Anthropic researchers that rapidly progressing artificial intelligence could lead to the extinction of the human race in the not-too-distant future. Fuente: France 24 - English.
item.dc:creator: FRANCE24

item.title: Study reveals link between Tibetan Plateau heat and record rain in California
item.description: Abnormally high temperatures across the Tibetan Plateau in early winter can trigger catastrophic rainstorms in California, according to a new study revealing a previously unidentified climate connection. In the winters of 2016-2017 and 2022-2023, record-breaking rain swept across the US state and surrounding areas, causing billions of dollars in damage and several deaths during years when drier weather was expected in the region. A study led by researchers from the University of California, Los... Fuente: South China Morning Post.
item.dc:creator: Victoria Bela

item.title: Uniting sequence and structure to map the protein universe across billions of years of evolution
item.description: An international team of researchers, including those at the Earth-Life Science Institute (ELSI) at the Institute of Science Tokyo, has developed a protein language model that brings together two fundamental sources of information about proteins: their amino acid sequences and three-dimensional structures. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Research shows agricultural fungicides drive evolution of multidrug resistance in soil microbes
item.description: Two newly published studies from Trinity College Dublin scientists raise significant concerns about the use of agricultural fungicides.That is because they show fungicides can rapidly drive soil microbes to evolve multidrug resistance to clinically important drugs and, when combined with warmer temperatures, disrupt soil microbes in ways that negatively affect plant growth. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: When a company 'believes' something false that causes harm, who's to blame? Professor offers a new answer
item.description: When Boeing certified the 737 Max in 2017 as safe to fly, a flight-control system it had approved caused two crashes that killed 346 people. When Takata kept shipping airbag inflators it had cleared for use, the devices exploded on impact, triggering the largest automotive recall in U.S. history. When a Hollywood armorer handed Alec Baldwin a gun on the set of "Rust," she believed it held no live rounds, but it did, and the shot killed cinematographer Halyna Hutchins. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Planes on a snake? Scientists discover various crab species hitching rides on sea snakes
item.description: Like all other snakes, sea snakes shed their skin as they grow. But because they live near the surface of the open ocean, they don't have the benefit of removing their old skin by slithering against a hard surface. Instead, they wriggle into a pretzel and use the friction generated by their scales to get the job done. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Low-cost phone lessons keep children learning during emergency school closures across five countries
item.description: The COVID-19 pandemic lockdowns forced people to find ways to get things done remotely. Companies developed systems that made working from home run smoothly. Educators also had to shift to mobile phones and group video calls to get their lessons across and make sure students didn't lose out on their progress. This exposed the need for education systems to be more resilient and adaptive to local and global disruptions. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A new surface atlas of Phobos will help MMX mission collect its samples
item.description: Thanks to JAXA, the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency, and its sample-return capabilities, we're on the cusp of receiving our first sample from the Martian system—not from Mars itself, but from its largest moon, Phobos. JAXA's Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) mission is set to launch in October. It will reach Phobos in 2027 and, if successful, return a sample from the moon to Earth in 2031. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Trump dismisses AI extinction risks as more than a dozen OpenAI, Anthropic insiders call for a slowdown
item.description: Trump said he isn't concerned AI could cause human extinction as researchers at leading AI companies warn about rapid advances and lawmakers propose safeguards. Fuente: CNBC - World.

item.title: Ocean acidification may disrupt diatoms' carbon capture and marine food webs
item.description: Our oceans are in trouble, and new research from Flinders University shows how changes in diatoms (microalgae) could further undermine the foundation of aquatic food webs—as well as vital deep-sea carbon capture or sequestration. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: eROSITA's second data release catalog delivering most comprehensive high-energy census of the cosmos to date
item.description: The eROSITA (extended ROentgen Survey with an Imaging Telescope Array) telescope, the primary instrument aboard the Russian-German Spektr-RG space observatory, was developed by the Max Planck Institute for Extraterrestrial Physics (MPE) and collaborators to study the soft X-ray night sky. The mission launched in 2019 and has delivered deep, sharp images over very large areas of the sky to map the high-energy universe. This past summer, the German eROSITA Consortium made its second data release (DR2), the most comprehensive catalog of the X-ray universe ever released. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Dogs and cats carry antibiotic-resistant bacteria also found in people, study finds
item.description: Dogs and cats may carry strains of Klebsiella pneumoniae, a potentially serious bacterium that can cause infections and is also found in humans, according to new research from Bournemouth University published in the journal Transboundary and Emerging Diseases. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: When AI designs the product, consumers have doubts
item.description: A new study from Georgia State University's J. Mack Robinson College of Business and the University of South Florida delivers a pointed warning to companies betting on AI to power their product design: The technology may make products more efficient, but it doesn't necessarily make consumers believe they are more sustainable. In fact, it can do the opposite. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Too much light at night may quietly reshape your heart
item.description: Nighttime light exposure was linked to thicker, stiffer heart chambers and early signs of reduced heart function in a study of more than 11,000 people. The findings suggest that keeping bedrooms darker could be an overlooked strategy for protecting the heart. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: El secreto de la extinción aviar estaba escondido en el lugar más insospechado: un excremento de dinosaurio
item.description: Hay ocasiones en las que los descubrimientos paleontológicos más revolucionarios no provienen de un esqueleto completo y perfectamente articulado, sino de los lugares más glamurosos. Para ver un ejemplo de esta situación, nos tenemos que ir hasta 2016, cuando un equipo de investigadores halló en la famosa formación de Hell Creek un excremento fosilizado. Y aunque todo parecía apuntar a que solo era una deposición de un dinosaurio carnívoro del Cretácico Superior, la realidad es que ha resultado ser una cápsula del tiempo. Su análisis. Tras hacer este descubrimiento, los investigadores… Fuente: Xataka.
item.dc:creator: José A. Lizana

item.title: 'Ex-Utero' project uses art, science to explore regenerative medicine
item.description: On a sunny spring day at Penn State, Cristin Millett, professor of art in the College of Arts and Architecture's School of Visual Arts, inserted a catheter needle into the umbilical vein of a placenta. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Your next prescription could be treating a side effect from the last one
item.description: A major Ontario study found 24 common medication chains in which one drug’s side effects can be mistaken for a new medical problem, leading to another prescription. Researchers say closer medication reviews, pharmacist involvement, and automated alerts could help prevent these potentially harmful prescribing cascades. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: What the backlash to the Industrial Revolution can teach us about handcrafts in the age of AI
item.description: Artificial intelligence (AI) isn't yet causing widespread job losses in Australia. But with some high-profile business leaders still predicting a looming unemployment "crisis," it's little wonder many people fear AI is coming for their job. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New analysis reconstructs the dawn of dinosaurs and other reptiles
item.description: About 252 million years ago, at the end of the Permian Period, a large proportion of species on Earth rapidly became extinct. After this mass extinction, many groups of organisms began to recover, while reptiles known as archosauromorphs—the group that includes dinosaurs and crocodiles—proliferated. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scientists just made quantum computer operations 1,000 times faster
item.description: Researchers have found a way to perform certain quantum operations more than 1,000 times faster, cutting thousands of repeated control cycles down to just one. The advance could reduce errors and bring reliable, fault-tolerant quantum computers closer to reality. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Can people truly walk away from terrorism? Inside the slow work of rehabilitation
item.description: As we reflect on the 25 years since the 9/11 terrorist attacks that killed almost 3,000 people, terrorism remains an ongoing yet evolving threat that defies easy answers. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Wasps are disappearing this summer, and scientists are worried
item.description: Britain’s wasps have become mysteriously scarce this summer, and scientists suspect an unusual combination of temperature swings, heatwaves, and food shortages may be responsible. Even the wasps that remain appear unusually small, potentially offering a glimpse of how extreme heat could reshape insect populations. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: La Guardia Civil buscaba al mayor estafador inmobiliario de Mallorca. Lo encontraron escondido debajo del fregadero de casa de su madre
item.description: Nueve meses en busca y captura, y la Guardia Civil lo encontró donde empezó todo: en casa de su madre, en Calella (Barcelona), escondido en un mueble bajo el fregadero . Carlos García Roldán, 'Charly' para sus víctimas, es el cerebro de Lujo Casa, la mayor estafa inmobiliaria investigada en Baleares: 3,4 millones de euros sustraídos a al menos 235 compradores mediante viviendas que nunca existieron. La Audiencia Provincial lo condenó en diciembre a casi 15 años de cárcel. Él, simplemente, no se presentó a firmar la sentencia. Cómo dieron con él. Los investigadores de la Guardia Civil… Fuente: Xataka.
item.dc:creator: Isra Fdez

item.title: Study of 1.9 million people finds a striking link between ADHD and gut problems
item.description: Researchers analyzing data from more than 1.9 million people found that ADHD is associated with substantially higher rates of digestive problems. People with ADHD had nearly double the odds of constipation, 58% higher odds of irritable bowel syndrome, and more than four times the odds of encopresis. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: How western consumption becomes the Global South's environmental nightmare
item.description: Industrialized countries send millions of metric tonnes of used clothing, electronic equipment and other products to the Global South, along with the environmental and health costs tied to producing, consuming and disposing of those goods. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: La UE y Ucrania lanzan una alianza industrial para acelerar la producción de drones
item.description: La Alianza de Drones UE-Ucrania dedicada a acelerar el desarrollo conjunto de las capacidades europeas en el campo de las armas no tripuladas , aprovechando la experiencia del combate activo, acaba de constituirse formalmente en Bruselas bajo la presidencia del comisario europeo de Defensa, Andrius Kubilius. La junta está compuesta por representantes de 18 empresas, la mitad europeas y la otra mitad ucranianas. Además, la Comisión ha anunciado que ha desbloqueado 6.100 millones de euros destinados a la compra de misiles Patriot para la defensa antiaérea ucraniana, entre otros los cohetes que… Fuente: ABC España - Internacional.

item.title: Maine's sugar kelp reveals four distinct populations vital for restoration
item.description: Saccharina latissima, or sugar kelp, is one of the dominant species in Maine's kelp forests, providing food, habitat and clean water to support a rich marine ecosystem. It is also the bedrock of the state's burgeoning kelp aquaculture industry, which relies on the annual harvest of reproductive tissue from the wild. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Why fears of AI self-improvement are causing ‘existential’ concerns at Anthropic and OpenAI
item.description: AI researchers are warning that faster AI self-improvement could eventually make advanced systems harder for humans to control. Fuente: CNBC - World.

item.title: Blue light breaks long-standing chemistry rule, unlocking 3D drug building blocks
item.description: For more than a century, pharmaceutical companies have relied on flat structures called aromatic rings, which can help drugs bind to target sites in the body. They include benzene rings and other flat, nitrogen-containing rings. But there are limits to their usefulness. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scientist finds 10,000-year-old mastodon molar while surveying California creek for threatened frogs
item.description: While investigating a creek for frogs, a scientist stumbled upon a remarkable ancient mastodon tooth, estimated to be over ten thousand years old. Paleontologists have confirmed its belonging to a long-extinct species of Pacific mastodon. The fossil will soon be analyzed at Stanford University to determine its precise age, establishing a fascinating connection between today's conservation initiatives and the ancient ecosystems of California. Fuente: The Times of India - World.

item.title: Did the War on Terror succeed? Or did Washington fall into al Qaeda’s trap?
item.description: PRESS REVIEW: Friday, September 11– 25 years on from 9/11, the international press reflects on the war on terror, its legacy and its failings. In France, the far-right National Rally party tries desperately to distance itself from the overtly racist comments of one of its security officials, made while on duty for his day job as a police officer. Finally, a fossilised feather may give us new insights into why birds survived the asteroid that killed the dinosaurs. Fuente: France 24 - English.
item.dc:creator: Antonia KERRIGAN

item.title: Snake grows a fake spider on its tail to lure birds; scans reveal surprisingly normal bones inside
item.description: Researchers utilized XCT scanning technology to investigate the unique tail of a viper. The imaging uncovered the presence of standard viper vertebrae within the tail's unusual form. This finding underscores the discrepancies that can exist between external appearance and internal skeletal makeup. Fossilized remains alone may not capture the true look of an organism, while museum specimens remain crucial for advancing our understanding through innovative methods. Fuente: The Times of India - World.
item.dc:creator: TOI Science Desk

item.title: Indonesia seeks to bring back baby orangutans allegedly trafficked to India
item.description: Indonesian authorities are working to repatriate five baby orangutans allegedly trafficked to India, where they were found motherless in a forest, Jakarta's forestry ministry told AFP on Friday. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A team of teams like never before: rehearsing a unique launch at ESA mission control
item.description: On 15 September, two spacecraft will leave Earth together aboard the same launcher from Europe’s spaceport in Kourou: FLEX, ESA’s photosynthesis mission, and Sentinel-3C, Copernicus’ newest satellite monitoring Earth’s oceans, land, ice and atmosphere. At ESA’s European Space Operations Centre (ESOC), two independent mission teams are preparing to operate the spacecraft in parallel in a closely coordinated effort. As launch approaches, they are rehearsing side by side to prepare not only for their own missions, but also for the moments when the two operations intersect. Fuente: European Space Agency.

item.title: Researchers eye AI revolution in natural disaster forecasts
item.description: A revolution in forecasting natural disasters is underway, say researchers in Switzerland who are training AI models using vast troves of NASA climate data to produce potentially lifesaving data at lightning speed. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: China y Rusia tienen un plan extremadamente ambicioso: en 2028 construirán una central nuclear en la Luna
item.description: Yuri Ivánovich Borísov, exviceministro de Defensa de Rusia y actualmente al frente de Roscosmos, la agencia espacial rusa, confirmó en marzo de 2024 que China y el país liderado por Vladímir Putin planeaban instalar un reactor nuclear en la superficie de la Luna . La dilatada experiencia de Rusia en el desarrollo de infraestructuras nucleares está fuera de toda duda. Y China, aunque ha llegado más tarde a esta industria, tiene la capacidad científica y los recursos necesarios para salir airosa. Su plan pasa por tener lista en 2035 la Estación Internacional de Investigación Lunar (conocida… Fuente: Xataka.

item.title: War, sanctions and inflation leave Iran short of hundreds of medicines
item.description: Prices for basic medicines such as paracetamol and insulin have skyrocketed amid major shortages of less common pharmaceuticals. More than 70% of healthcare costs in Iran are paid out of pocket, leaving the most vulnerable patients unable to afford treatment. Fuente: Euronews.

item.title: Physicists just found a tiny glitch in time itself
item.description: Unconventional quantum theories may imply that time itself has a tiny fundamental uncertainty, placing an ultimate limit on how precisely any clock could measure it. The effect is far beyond current detection, but it could reveal a hidden connection between quantum mechanics, gravity, and spacetime. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Scientists find signs of extreme aging and youth in the same 117-year-old
item.description: A remarkably detailed study of Maria Branyas, who lived past 117, reveals that extreme longevity may involve both intense aging and powerful biological protection at the same time. Researchers found signs of advanced aging, but also low inflammation, beneficial gut bacteria, protective genetic features, and a biological age younger than her chronological age. Because she avoided major disease, the study offered a rare look at aging itself rather than the illnesses that often accompany it. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.description: Mexico’s second-largest metropolitan area borders on folded rock layers of the Sierra Madre Oriental. Fuente: NASA.

item.title: DRC's cobalt exports contain unreported uranium—our study estimates the global nuclear risk
item.description: The southern region of the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) is known as the Copperbelt because of its rich deposits of copper and other minerals. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scientists discover the human heart can regrow muscle after a heart attack
item.description: Researchers have shown for the first time that human heart muscle cells can regrow after a heart attack. The finding overturns the idea that damaged areas of the heart are completely incapable of regeneration. Scientists now hope to identify ways to dramatically boost this natural repair process, potentially opening a new path toward treatments for heart failure. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: London misperceptions: Study reveals what Britons get wrong
item.description: London has one of the lowest violent crime rates of any region in England and Wales, tops a global ranking of the best cities, and pays more in taxes than it receives back in public spending—but the public overestimates how likely Londoners are to become victims of crime, underestimates the capital's international standing, and has little idea it is the key contributor to public finances, according to a new study from the Policy Institute at King's College London. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Eating only 8 hours a day may help control Type 1 diabetes
item.description: Eating only between noon and 8 p.m. improved blood sugar control in a small study of adults with Type 1 diabetes and obesity, while avoiding an increase in serious complications. The promising findings offer the first evidence that time restricted eating could become another tool for managing the condition. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: English, but make it TikTok: How social media is reshaping language
item.description: Give, eat, cook and serve are everyday English words. On TikTok, they're doing something different. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: The Moon may have formed intact just hours after a giant collision
item.description: Scientists have discovered that the Moon-forming collision may have depended heavily on how hot and physically strong early Earth and Theia were. New simulations found that some impacts create the familiar disk of debris that later becomes the Moon, while others can produce an intact Moon in only about five hours. The results challenge the long-standing assumption that the enormous collision could be modeled as if both worlds behaved mostly like fluids. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Fast-growing money market funds linked to 'exuberant' equity markets and systemic risk
item.description: Money market funds (MMFs) that grow rapidly when equity markets are soaring pose a systemic risk to global financial systems, new academic research reveals. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: UCLA scientists turn cord blood into powerful cancer-fighting T cells
item.description: UCLA researchers developed ready-made cancer-fighting T cells from cord blood stem cells that can attack solid tumors through two separate detection systems. In mice, a single dose controlled cancer and extended survival while avoiding a dangerous complication associated with donor-derived T-cell therapies. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: The hunt for unknown life in New York City
item.description: The globe is full of unknown species. But is it really possible to find a completely new animal species in the middle of the largest city in the United States? Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scientists visualize proteins' hidden water architecture that may help define biological function
item.description: For decades, scientists have understood proteins primarily through two defining features: their amino acid sequence and their three-dimensional structure. This framework has driven major advances in biology, biotechnology and medicine, culminating in recent artificial intelligence tools capable of predicting protein structures with remarkable accuracy. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Global database reveals why no two cities' food emissions look the same
item.description: Switching to a more sustainable diet could halve food-related emissions in cities such as Amsterdam, while in cities such as Dhaka and Delhi, the focus should be more on making food production more sustainable as they widen food access. A new database by Leiden researchers shows that different cities need different approaches to achieve a more sustainable food system. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: What drove the Tasmanian devil out of northern WA?
item.description: Researchers say Tasmanian devils lived alongside humans in WA's arid Pilbara for tens of thousands of years, and the arrival of the dingo may have disrupted that relationship. Fuente: ABC News Australia.
item.dc:creator: Amy Rossbach

item.title: Rare bird fossils from Bavaria reveal new species, including an eagle
item.description: The Hammerschmiede clay pit near Pforzen in the eastern Allgäu is famous for its wealth of finds: Besides fossils of two early anthropoid apes, the remains of numerous vertebrate species have been uncovered in 11.6-million-year-old river sediments—but until now, very few birds. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Has gentle parenting gone too far?
item.description: To be or not to be a gentle parent? That is the question. There is so much controversy these days about gentle parenting. What is it, and what is it not? Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Q&A: The overlooked networks of heat resilience within communities
item.description: As extreme heat becomes more frequent and severe, many people are turning to informal adaptation strategies—rigging up plastic sheeting overhead for shade, sharing water at a community tap and creating neighborhood cooling areas. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Under pressure: How a deep-sea protein adapts to an extreme environment
item.description: Life in the deep sea is under immense pressure—literally. Such extreme conditions can disrupt the delicate structures of proteins essential to life. Yet somehow, the proteins in deep-sea creatures remain functional. This raises an intriguing question: how? Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: 25 years after 9/11, research traces changing landscape of religious bias
item.description: A quarter-century after the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks, religious bias in America has not disappeared, but the forces shaping it have changed. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Future catastrophic weather could be 'far worse' than history suggests
item.description: Historical records of the deadliest storms and heat waves may be a poor indicator of the scale and impact future weather disasters could have, scientists at King's College London warn. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: How to help your garden recover from a heat wave
item.description: UK gardens took a battering this summer as a heat dome settled over western Europe, and much of the green and pleasant land turned a dusty beige. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Cell wall transport disruption exposes weakness in antibiotic-resistant bacteria
item.description: Even highly antibiotic-resistant bacteria become more vulnerable when their cell wall transport system is disrupted, according to a new study from Umeå University. The discovery reveals a previously overlooked weakness that could help researchers develop new strategies to combat antibiotic resistance. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Psychologist wins Ig Nobel for proving rich drivers are the worst
item.description: Paul K. Piff, UC Irvine associate professor of psychology, has officially been recognized for what millions of frustrated commuters have long suspected: The fancier the car, the worse the driver. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Fully recyclable hydrogel begins healing itself within minutes
item.description: Imagine this. You pick up a contact lens from its container and—yikes!—it falls on the bathroom floor. Before you know it, your cat pounces, claws out. By the time you wrestle it back, the lens looks like a tiny chew toy. And then, just like that—the scratches fade away and the ripped edge seals itself up. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Learning without a brain—how bacteria store memories and remember the past like artificial neural networks
item.description: Learning is often thought to require a brain. But learning is a broad concept that does not necessarily depend on neurons. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: 'CRISPR-Combo' system speeds regeneration of hard-to-breed perennial crops
item.description: Editing a plant's genes is only half the battle. Before a new, improved trait can ever reach a farmer's field, scientists must be able to grow a whole plant from just a few edited cells—a process that can be slow, unreliable and, for some plant species, impossible. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Portland report maps complex journeys through homelessness
item.description: A new report from Portland State University's Homelessness Research and Action Collaborative (HRAC) and the OHSU-PSU School of Public Health offers an in-depth examination of how individuals navigate, survive and attempt to exit homelessness in Multnomah County. Titled "Without a Map: A Lived Experience Study of the Paths People Create Through Homelessness," the publication serves as the second and final part of the Pathways study. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.description: The Republic of Djibouti will sign the Artemis Accords during a ceremony at 11 a.m. EDT, Monday, Sept. 14, at NASA Headquarters in Washington, becoming the 72nd country signatory. NASA Deputy Administrator Matt Anderson will host Ambassador of Djibouti to the United States Mohamed Siad Douale for the ceremony, together with U.S. State Department Assistant […] Fuente: NASA.

item.title: New genomic tool for clams boosts sustainable aquaculture
item.description: An international team of researchers, including CIIMAR, has developed a new tool that could help produce clams that are more resistant to disease and climate change while also strengthening the conservation of these species' genetic diversity. The study, published in the journal Aquaculture, represents a significant step forward for sustainable aquaculture and the management of two of the most economically important clam species: the Japanese clam (Ruditapes philippinarum) and the good clam (Ruditapes decussatus). Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Global study reveals hidden nutritional value of shellfish and other aquatic invertebrates
item.description: The nutritional value of aquatic invertebrates such as oysters, mussels and crabs has been significantly overlooked, according to a new study led by researchers at King Abdullah University of Science and Technology (KAUST). The findings provide one of the most comprehensive assessments to date of the nutritional contribution of aquatic invertebrates, along with new evidence to better understand their role in human nutrition and help inform more sustainable fisheries, aquaculture and food-system planning. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Unveiling how nanoparticles create iridescence in ancient ceramics
item.description: Scientists led by the Universitat Politècnica de Barcelona and the ESRF, the European Synchrotron, have revealed the chemical reactions in nanoparticles that created a unique, shimmering effect in the painting on ninth-century Islamic ceramics. The results are published in Science Advances. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: How sex with multiple mates can help save species from extinction
item.description: Allowing females to mate with multiple males, rather than just one, could help make species more resistant to extinction, University of East Anglia research shows. A new study reveals that when females have multiple males to mate with, their offspring inherit significantly fewer harmful genetic mutations. This, in turn, makes the entire population healthier and less likely to die out. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Supercomputer simulations reveal how the molecular motor kinesin steers itself along tracks
item.description: Kinesin is a molecular motor responsible for hauling essential cargoes within cells by walking step by step along filamentous tracks known as microtubules. To move efficiently and avoid falling off, the motor's two feet must coordinate their stepping in a precise direction. Scientists have known that a connecting segment called the neck region is crucial for coordinating this motion. However, its exact three-dimensional structure and how it physically interacts with the microtubule track have remained a mystery because of the limitations of current imaging techniques. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA Answers President’s Call to Establish United States Space Academy
item.description: Less than two weeks after an Executive Order was signed to create the first United States Space Academy, NASA-led work is in full swing to make the academy a reality and shape the future of America’s aerospace workforce and leadership. NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman chaired the first Presidential Commission on the United States Space Academy […] Fuente: NASA.

item.title: Ancient Swedish Goths had surprisingly accurate calendars
item.description: On a mostly flat plain an hour north of Stockholm lies a collection of large burial mounds dating from an ancient culture at least 2,500 years old. These people were not Vikings; they were northern Germanic Goths, pagan polytheists worshiping the precursors of Odin, Freyr and Thor. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: An unusual bacterium that penetrates and lives inside human cells may offer a new drug target
item.description: Research underway in the lab of Rebecca Alexander, a professor in Wake Forest University's Department of Chemistry, is shedding light on an unusual human bacterium, Mycoplasma penetrans. Alexander's work to understand how and why this unique pathogen acts as it does could one day lead to new classes of drugs that better target illnesses associated with this particular pathogen, as well as others that act similarly. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.description: Search and rescue technology developed in part by NASA saved five lives Fuente: NASA.

item.title: What small insects can tell us about ancient textiles
item.description: Anna Sheinberg, Ph.D. candidate in chemistry, is working with fellow researchers in Trinity College's Chemistry Department and at the Nasher Museum of Art to uncover new information about some of the ancient dyed textiles in the Nasher's collection. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Rethinking how household income needs are assessed for welfare support
item.description: How much more income does a two-person household need than a person living alone? The answer is not simply twice as much. Two people need more food and other necessities, but they can also share expenses such as housing. This means that as a household grows, the income needed to maintain the same standard of living increases—but usually by less than the number of people in the household. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: From flower to fruit: A tug-of-war between growing tissues
item.description: Unlike an animal cell, a plant cell can't crawl or migrate. It's locked inside a rigid wall, cemented to its neighbors for life. A cell born at the center of a young fruit will still be there when that fruit ripens. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Climate hazards disrupted schooling for more than 171 million students in 2025
item.description: More than 171 million students globally—or 1 in 10—from preprimary to upper secondary age had their schooling disrupted by climate hazards in 2025, according to a new analysis released by UNICEF today. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Kids' brains are built for distraction. Sometimes that's a good thing.
item.description: Parents often learn the hard way that to make it anywhere on time, they should calculate how much time they think they need to get ready—and double it. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Tightly guided atoms could enable low-power quantum navigation when GPS fails
item.description: Within tiny halos of light clinging to a vanishingly thin wisp of optical fiber, scientist Jongmin Lee guides atoms like marbles through a narrow pipe. Rock the fiber and the atoms shift side by side; they just don't fall off. But don't be deceived by the seemingly delicate nature of his experiment. Lee is exploring how to measure motion precisely in rough-and-tumble environments. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: First PLP-dependent enzyme that influences bacterial protein production discovered
item.description: Researchers from the Singapore-MIT Alliance for Research & Technology's (SMART) Antimicrobial Resistance (AMR) interdisciplinary research group, alongside collaborators from Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), Nanyang Technological University (NTU Singapore), and institutions in the United States, Poland and France, have discovered aminovaleramididine synthetase (AvaS), the first identified pyridoxal phosphate (PLP)-dependent enzyme responsible for producing a chemical modification linked to how bacteria respond to metabolic stress. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.description: Europe is looking inward, and perhaps to China, as the White House tries to cancel some NASA partnerships. Fuente: Ars Technica.

item.title: La NASA quiere entender mejor la Luna antes de volver allí. Ha creado con IBM una IA para encontrar hielo y nuevos cráteres
item.description: Durante 17 años, la Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter ha fotografiado y medido la Luna hasta construir uno de los archivos más detallados que existen sobre su superficie. La NASA asegura que la misión ha generado un volumen de datos mayor que el de todas sus demás misiones planetarias combinadas , con una cobertura que permite observar buena parte del terreno lunar a gran resolución. El problema ya no es solo obtener información, sino procesarla con suficiente rapidez para extraer de ella patrones útiles. Y esa tarea gana peso mientras la agencia prepara el regreso de astronautas a la superficie… Fuente: Xataka.
item.dc:creator: Javier Marquez

item.title: Muscovite identified as a low-index building block for ultrathin van der Waals photonic components
item.description: Researchers have demonstrated that a naturally occurring mineral can serve as a low-loss optical material for next-generation broadband all–van der Waals nanophotonic components. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Ultrathin silicon structures can tune mid-IR light in billionths of a second
item.description: Light in the mid-infrared (mid-IR) portion of the electromagnetic spectrum plays a key role in modern sensing. Because molecules interact with this kind of light in specific ways, researchers use technologies like mid-IR spectroscopy to identify biological materials, drugs and pollutants. Mid-IR light can also serve as a carrier of information in free-space optical communications, where data are transmitted through the air without using cables or fibers. Better control of mid-IR light could therefore lead to more sensitive detectors and faster communications. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.description: Some 550 million years ago, Earth looked very different than it does today. The Southern Hemisphere was dominated by an enormous single continent known as Gondwana. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: River erosion explains uneven crustal uplift across Basque-Cantabrian Range
item.description: A University of the Basque Country-EHU research group has determined the causes of a 255 m (837 feet) crustal uplift of the Atlantic slope and a 167 m (548 feet) uplift of the Mediterranean slope, as well as the development of rivers in these areas. Fuente: Phys.org.
